description: A crash course in Georgia's DPH pool rules for swimming pools, spas and water parks, and the rules that may create a legal duty when a child is hurt.
shortAnswer: Every legal claim starts with an analysis of what duty was violated. In Georgia the State agency that is tasked with oversight of pools, spas, and recreational water parks is DPH, and a working knowledge of the rules made by that agency will help you discover what duties might apply to your situation.

faq.q: Which pools are exempt from Georgia's DPH pool rules?
faq.a: The DPH rules are limited in scope. Private pools and hot tubs/spas, apartment complex pools, country club pools, and subdivision pools that are open only to residents of the subdivision and their guests are expressly exempt, and there are a few other categories of pools/spas/baths that fall outside the scope of the DPH rules.

faq.q: What kind of barrier does Georgia require around a public pool?
faq.a: All outdoor swimming pools and spas shall be provided with a barrier. The top of the barrier must be at least four feet high. All access gates must be self-latching. Pedestrian access gates must also be self-closing.

faq.q: What lifesaving equipment must a Georgia pool have?
faq.a: Requirements include, but are not limited to, a pole not less than 12 feet long, including a body hook; a throwing rope to which has been firmly attached a ring buoy; and a telephone which is hard wired and affixed (not a cell phone) with posted names and numbers for emergency personnel.

faq.q: Are the state DPH rules the only source of pool safety duties in Georgia?
faq.a: DPH is not the ONLY source of duties that might apply to your situation. Many Georgia counties have county pool regulations. Federal law creates other duties (such as the Federal Pool and Spa Safety Act of 2007).
